articles.summary: Finance Payroll Fraud in Nigeria: Common Risks and How Businesses Can Prevent Them Oluwakemi Adesina September 7, 2026 Payroll fraud in Nigeria is usually one of the last things businesses pay attention to and that sometimes makes it a prime target. Payroll often accounts for a large share of operating costs, in service-based businesses it can run well above 40 percent, which makes it one of the biggest items on the books. Unlike procurement fraud, which usually surfaces through a missing delivery or a mismatched invoice, payroll fraud can run quietly for months because nothing about it looks out of place. This guide shows you how payroll fraud happens in Nigeria, how to spot it early, and what controls protect your business. What Is Payroll Fraud? Payroll fraud occurs when someone manipulates payroll to move money the business did not authorise. It can involve inflated payments, fake employees, or redirected salaries. Most times, it is an inside job because the person already knows the process and has access. Phishing, fake contractor payments, and vendor invoice fraud are real threats. But most payroll losses come from employees or admins with payroll access. As your business grows, informal processes that worked with 10 staff can break down at 50. Common Types of Payroll Fraud in Nigeria These fraud patterns show up in businesses of every size. Most do not need technical skill, just access and weak checks: Ghost Employees: A ghost employee is a name on the payroll with no real person behind it. It may be entirely fabricated or belong to a former employee who was never properly offboarded. If payroll removal and access revocation do not happen on the final day of employment, salaries can continue to be deposited into a bank account controlled by someone else. Falsified Overtime Claims: Overtime fraud occurs when hours never worked are submitted and approved. The risk is higher when overtime authorisation happens through informal messages or verbal sign-offs, especially for shift workers, field staff, or project teams where hours are hard to verify against output. Unauthorised Salary Increases: A salary adjustment made outside the formal review cycle without required management approval is an unauthorised increase. The risk is particularly high when the person managing employee records can also run payroll. Manipulated Bank Account Details: An administrator or employee may change a bank account number shortly before a pay run. The payroll figures still look correct, but the money is sent elsewhere. Without a process that verifies every change to bank details before payment, this can go undetected. Duplicate Salary Payments: Processing the same payroll twice or paying an employee through two channels in the same cycle creates duplicate disbursements. Manual payroll or disconnected systems increase this risk when payments are not followed by reconciliation. Payroll Data Manipulation: This includes adjusting salary figures, inflating reimbursements, or manipulating tax and pension deductions. One serious example is under-remitting statutory deductions: PAYE or pension is deducted from salaries as normal, but a lower amount is remitted to the relevant authority, and the difference is redirected. Warning Signs of Payroll Fraud Nigeria Businesses Should Watch Payroll Costs Rising Without your Headcount Growth If the salary bill increases while the headcount stays stable, investigate. A month-on-month comparison of payroll spend against active headcount can help identify unexplained growth and possible ghost employee activity. Frequent Last-Minute Payroll Changes New bank details, revised figures, or additional names submitted close to processing time are harder to scrutinise. They are not automatically fraudulent, but recurring late changes should be documented and reviewed. Bank Account Changes Without Verification Every employee bank-account update should require independent verification before a live pay run. Direct confirmation through a channel outside the payroll team’s control adds an important check. Overtime Patterns With No Operational Explanation If overtime is concentrated among a small group without a documented project, deadline, or business event to explain it, cross-check claims against attendance, output, or project records. Missing or Informal Approval Records Every salary addition, change, and disbursement should have a signed, dated, traceable approval record. WhatsApp messages, verbal conversations, or missing records create gaps in the audit trail. Duplicate Employee Records Different name variations, staff IDs, or bank accounts for the same employee require investigation. It may be an administrative error or a sign of a ghost employee scheme. Payroll Internal Controls That Close the Gaps The key is a process where more than one person reviews the numbers before money moves. Payroll compliance and fraud prevention rely on many of the same controls. Segregation of Duties The person who sets up a payroll run should not approve it or release the payment. Where teams are small, the minimum fix is to have final payment approval handled by someone outside the payroll function. Multi-Level Approval Workflows Every payroll run should require documented sign-off from more than one person. Salary changes, new hires, exits, and amendments should also require authorisation from someone who did not make the change. Approval by WhatsApp alone is not a reliable audit trail. Role-Based System Access System permissions should match job responsibilities. The administrator managing employee records should not authorise payments, the payroll processor should not freely edit salary figures, and an approved payroll run should not be editable by the approver. Verified Employee Records Every active payroll entry should correspond to a current, verified employee, with up-to-date employment records and verified bank details. Cross-checking pension deduction records with PenCom can also help verify employees and confirm that statutory obligations are being met. Payroll Audit Trails Every payroll change should be timestamped, attributed to a specific user, and retained in a log that cannot be edited after the fact. If you cannot identify who changed a bank account or salary figure and when, you are missing a basic fraud-detection mechanism. How Payroll Audits Reduce Payroll Fraud Risks A payroll audit is a scheduled, independent review of payroll data against HR records, approval logs, and statutory remittances. Its purpose is to verify that payments were authorised and deductions

articles.summary: Employee Management Employee Leave Management in Nigeria: Best Practices for HR and Payroll Teams Oluwakemi Adesina September 17, 2026 Employee leave management in Nigeria needs more structure as businesses grow because the process eventually outgrows spreadsheets, WhatsApp messages, and informal approvals. This guide covers what proper leave management requires, what the law says, how leave connects to payroll accuracy, and how to build a system that scales. What Is Employee Leave Management? Employee leave management is the process of tracking, approving, recording, and reconciling employee time off across all leave types and pay cycles. It connects HR administration to payroll processing and workforce planning. The objective is straightforward: ensure employees receive the correct leave entitlements, that every approved absence is documented, and that payroll reflects what actually happened. For Nigerian businesses, leave management also has a compliance dimension because minimum leave entitlements must be honoured. Types of Employee Leave in Nigeria A clear employee leave policy starts with defining the leave types the business recognises. Annual Leave: The Federal Ministry of Labour mandates a minimum of six working days of paid annual leave after 12 months of continuous service, though many employers provide more. Annual leave also requires coordination around schedules, cover, and accurate leave balances. Sick Leave: Sick leave in Nigeria is largely governed by employment contracts and internal policy. A written policy should define eligibility, approval, documentation, and what should be paid or deducted. Maternity Leave: Female employees are entitled to a minimum of 12 weeks of paid maternity leave under Nigerian labour law. The payroll treatment and supporting documentation should be clearly defined in policy and reflected accurately in the payroll system. Paternity Leave: Paternity leave is not currently mandated under federal labour law, but many employers provide it as a discretionary benefit. Where offered, eligibility, duration, and pay status should be documented. Compassionate Leave: Leave for bereavement or serious family emergencies should have clear rules covering circumstances, duration, and whether it is paid, partially paid, or unpaid. Study Leave: Study leave, whether paid or unpaid, should define eligibility, maximum duration, and how it interacts with annual leave or other benefits. Unpaid Leave: Unpaid leave requires clear rules for daily-rate deductions and pro-rated salary calculations. Inconsistent deductions are a recurring source of payroll disputes. Building an Employee Leave Policy That Works A leave policy is the operating framework that makes leave decisions consistent and understandable. Without one, managers make individual calls, employees develop different expectations, and HR spends time resolving preventable disputes. Eligibility and Entitlements: Define who qualifies for each leave type, when eligibility begins, whether contract staff have the same entitlement as permanent employees, and whether entitlement changes with tenure. Document these rules and communicate them at onboarding. Application and Approval Workflow: Define the application channel, approval timeline, approvers for each team, and what happens when the primary approver is unavailable. Verbal approvals or requests that never reach HR create gaps between what was approved and what payroll records show. Notice Requirements: Define notice periods for planned leave and a separate process for emergencies. Clear notice requirements support workforce planning and give HR time to update records before payroll runs. Carry-Forward Rules: Define whether unused annual leave carries forward, how much can be carried forward, for how long, and whether unused leave can be paid out. Clear year-end rules prevent disputes and unexpected financial obligations. Documentation Requirements: Every approved leave should generate a request, recorded approval, and updated leave balance. Policies should also specify documentation for sick and maternity leave. Employee leave records are a key source of payroll data, so incomplete records can produce incorrect pay. Where leave records intersect with statutory benefits, they should also be cross-referenced with relevant regulatory frameworks. How Employee Leave Management in Nigeria Affects Payroll Leave and payroll are closely connected. Every day of paid, unpaid, or partially paid leave can affect payroll, so HR and payroll teams need a shared and current record. Paid vs Unpaid Leave The distinction between paid and unpaid leave should be embedded in the payroll system rather than calculated manually at month end. Unpaid leave requires the correct daily-rate treatment based on the employee’s terms and the dates involved. Leave Balances and Payroll Reporting Payroll reporting should reconcile with leave balances. Outstanding annual leave, accrued leave liabilities, and possible leave encashment all depend on current leave records. Overtime and Cover Planning When employees are on leave, cover may involve internal reallocation or paid overtime. Effective leave tracking helps businesses plan cover, control overtime costs, and avoid unbudgeted costs. Leave Encashment Where unused annual leave is paid out, the encashment calculation should be accurate, auditable, and processed correctly through payroll. Clean leave records make the calculation straightforward. Common Leave Management Challenges in Nigerian Businesses Most challenges stem from a leave process designed for a small team that is stretched as the business grows. Manual tracking that does not scale. Multiple spreadsheets create conflicting versions and force HR and payroll teams to reconcile records by hand. Conflicting requests with no resolution framework. Without a written rule for competing leave requests, decisions can appear inconsistent or unfair. Approvals that never reach HR. A manager may approve leave verbally, while HR has no record of it, leading to payroll deductions and employee disputes. Leave records that do not match payroll records. Separate HR and payroll systems allow discrepancies to accumulate until payday. A policy that exists but is not communicated. Employees and managers improvise when leave rules are difficult to find or understand. Best Practices for Employee Leave Management in Nigeria Effective workforce leave management depends on consistent decisions, clear documentation, and accurate records. Write the policy before you need it. Cover entitlements, eligibility, application, approval workflow, notice, carry-forward, and payroll treatment. Keep employee leave records in one place. A single source of truth accessible to HR and payroll eliminates reconciliation gaps. Connect leave to payroll before the run. Leave data should inform payroll before processing, not be reconciled after salaries have been calculated. Review leave balances

articles.summary: Business Center How Do You Know If Your Business Is Ready to Scale? Oluwakemi Adesina September 22, 2026 Every founder dreams of growth, but what sets forward-thinking founders apart is that they plan for the capacity to carry it, well ahead of time. Growth can bring more customers, more revenue, bigger contracts and access to markets that once seemed out of reach. But growth also puts weight on every system underneath the business. The processes that felt perfectly adequate at 15 employees can buckle at 100. Financial records that worked with three revenue streams can become impossible to defend when a lender asks for a clear picture of margins. The informal way a founder managed people can collapse when the organisation becomes too large for everyone to know everyone else. That is the real test of growth, and it is normal. Think of it as a coming-of-age phase for every business, survivable by only the most resilient of businesses. Businesses that scale successfully in Nigeria’s changing economy are not necessarily the ones with the fewest problems. They also faced the myriad of problems Nigerian businesses face, but the defining thing about them, is that they identified the weaknesses that will come with their growth early and took care of those weaknesses before it grounded their business. At Eazipay, we see those weaknesses repeatedly across businesses at different stages of growth. They tend to concentrate in three areas: people infrastructure, cost structure and compliance framework. That’s why we call them the Three Growth Tests. So, if your business plans to hire significantly, serve more customers, raise capital, enter new markets or take on larger contracts, these are three areas worth testing before the next stage arrives. Get your results in 3 minutes Why readiness matters now For years, Nigerian businesses have had to spend significant management attention solving problems that had little to do with building the business itself. Founders navigated unpredictable foreign exchange access. Businesses worked around transaction limits. Cross-border payments created friction. Infrastructure problems raised operating costs. Teams stretched themselves across functions because building a fully staffed organisation was often harder than finding another workaround. So businesses adapted. They found alternative payment routes. They created manual processes. They kept records in different places. They asked one person to handle three functions because hiring three specialists did not make economic sense yet. Those adaptations helped keep businesses in motion. But they also created a habit that can become dangerous during the next phase of growth: solving each new problem as it appears instead of building a structure that prevents the same class of problems from returning. That distinction matters more as Nigeria’s business environment changes. In October 2025, the Financial Action Task Force removed Nigeria from its Grey List of jurisdictions under increased monitoring after concluding that Nigeria had completed the required action plan. The European Union subsequently removed Nigeria from its list of high-risk third countries through a regulation published in January 2026. Just around the same time, Nigeria’s new Tax Administration Act also took effect, introducing a new framework for tax administration and collection. These changes may seem unconnected, but they are. And while they all begin at the policy level, businesses experience them through practical questions. How easily can money move? How prepared are you to work with larger financial institutions? Can you satisfy the documentation requirements of a major customer? Can you produce reliable financial records when someone wants to invest or lend? Can your business handle a larger volume of transactions without creating new compliance problems? These questions are pertinent to the survival of your business as they determine how ready you are to meet the significant opportunity presented by these policy changes. These changes will bring about a more connected economy, and a more connected economy can give Nigerian businesses access to more customers, more capital, more trade and more opportunities to compete beyond the domestic market. But there’s a bigger catch. This opportunity also raises the standard your business must meet. That you have more room to grow is not the same as having the capacity to grow. That is where our Three Growth Tests come in. The first Growth Test: Is your people infrastructure ready? Early-stage businesses often run on adaptable generalists. That can be a strength, because when a company has ten or fifteen people, flexibility allows everyone to move quickly. The founder can step into recruitment when someone resigns, help finance when a payment needs approval and sit with operations when a customer issue needs solving. The business works because the people inside it compensate for the gaps in the structure. However, growth changes that equation. As headcount increases, the company needs more than hardworking people. It needs clarity about who owns what, how decisions get made and how the organisation develops and manages its people. That is what people infrastructure should provide. A strong people infrastructure gives the business: Clear job responsibilities and decision rights Defined performance expectations Consistent performance management and feedback Training, mentorship and leadership development Reliable workforce data for management decisions Structured payroll and employee administration Proper handling of applicable statutory obligations and benefits Systems that reduce unnecessary manual work The exact structure should match the business. That means a 15-person company does not need the same HR infrastructure as a 150-person organisation. But even then, the principle remains the same: the company needs to increase its ability to manage people at roughly the same pace it increases the number of people it employs. There’s another point to note here, which is that growth changes the kind of people you need. So, how does that happen? Why growth changes the kind of people you need Founders often underestimate the fact that growth does not simply require more people. It often requires different capabilities. A growing technology company may need experienced engineering leadership. A business entering enterprise markets may need people who understand procurement, contracts, compliance and risk. articles.summary: Business Center Payroll Internal Controls: How Nigerian Businesses Can Reduce Payroll Risks and Improve Compliance Oluwakemi Adesina September 17, 2026 Having a payroll process is not the same as having payroll internal controls. A process defines the steps: someone enters data, someone calculates payroll, someone approves it, and someone releases payment. Controls verify that the right things are happening at each stage. Payroll internal controls are the checks, segregation of duties, documented approvals, and system configurations that make it harder for errors and fraud to go undetected. For Nigerian businesses, where payroll can account for 30 to 60 percent of operating costs, getting this right is a financial priority. What Are Payroll Internal Controls? Payroll internal controls are the policies, procedures, and system configurations that verify payroll is accurate, authorised, and compliant at every stage. A payroll process defines what happens. Controls define who can do it, who checks it, and what happens when something is wrong. Payroll governance is the broader framework that keeps these controls working over time. A control that exists in a policy but is never enforced is not an effective control. The need becomes more obvious as businesses grow. At 15 employees, a founder may see the whole payroll. At 60 employees, that visibility is gone, but the informal process may remain unchanged. That gap is where many payroll risks begin. What Payroll Risks Look Like Without Controls Payroll risks often build up from small discrepancies, informal approvals, and unreconciled records. These are the main categories payroll security controls are designed to catch. Errors That Compound Quietly A leave balance not updated, a deduction applied to the wrong base, or a new employee added with an incorrect account number may seem minor. Across a team, repeated errors become payroll disputes, correction work, and lost employee trust. Fraud That Runs on Access Ghost employees, redirected salaries, and unauthorised pay increases often require access and the absence of an independent check. When one person can add an employee, set their salary, and release payment without review, the business is relying on trust rather than controls. Strong payroll controls should sit alongside broader financial crime prevention and anti-corruption practices. Compliance Failures That Arrive as Penalties Incorrect PAYE calculations, late pension remittances, or missing NHF contributions can create statutory risk even when the payroll output appears correct. Payroll compliance controls help businesses identify these issues before they become penalties. The Payroll Internal Controls That Do the Most Work Segregation of Duties The person who prepares the payroll run should not also approve it, and the approver should not release the payment. In smaller businesses, the minimum viable version is to ensure the person releasing the bank transfer did not prepare or approve the payroll. This independent check significantly reduces the risk of unchecked errors or fraud. Role-Based System Access Payroll security controls depend on limiting what each person can do in the system. The person entering salary data does not need payment approval rights, while an HR manager updating leave records may not need access to bank details. Permissions should match responsibilities rather than default to broad access. Documented Payroll Approval Workflow Every payroll run should follow a defined workflow: preparation, independent review, management sign-off, and payment release. Each stage should be logged, timestamped, attributed to a named user, and protected from later editing. An approval that happened only over WhatsApp is not a strong audit control. A documented workflow shows what was reviewed, who approved it, and when the approval happened. Employee Record Verification Before each payroll run, verify the active employee list against HR records. Confirm leavers have been removed, new starters have verified bank details, and records changed since the last run are flagged for review. This helps close gaps where ghost employees and bank-account manipulation can occur. Payroll Audit Trails Every salary amendment, bank-detail update, new employee addition, or deduction adjustment should generate an immutable log entry with a timestamp and user ID. Payroll audit controls provide the evidence needed to determine what changed, when, and who made the change. Payroll Reconciliation After every run, reconcile the total disbursed against the approved payroll schedule. Statutory remittances such as PAYE to FIRS, pension to PFAs, and NHF to FMBN should also be reconciled against what was calculated. Any difference should be investigated before the next cycle. How a Payroll Approval Workflow Actually Works A payroll approval workflow is a defined, documented sequence of authorisations, with each stage performed by an appropriate independent reviewer and logged in the system. Preparation: The payroll administrator builds the run from verified data, applies deductions, and flags anomalies before the review deadline. Independent review: A second person compares the current cycle with the previous one, checking payroll cost changes, recent bank-detail changes, new or removed employees, and other unusual items. Management sign-off: A finance director, COO, or business owner reviews the summary and provides documented approval. Payment release: The person releasing the bank transfer should be separate from preparation, review, and approval. Where full separation is not feasible, use dual authorisation. The value of the workflow is accountability. Each person is responsible for what they reviewed, making it more likely that anomalies receive proper attention. Payroll Monitoring: What Happens Between Audits Controls prevent problems from entering payroll, while payroll monitoring catches issues that get through and surfaces patterns before they become expensive. Useful exception reports flag unusual activity rather than simply summarising what was paid. Examples include payroll costs rising materially without headcount growth, sudden salary amendments, unexplained concentrations of overtime, or a new employee whose bank account matches an existing employee’s details. These are not automatically fraud. They are questions the payroll team should be able to answer. A payroll audit goes deeper by cross-checking the live employee list against HR records, verifying that statutory deductions were actually remitted, and reviewing the change log against documented approvals. For most Nigerian businesses, a quarterly audit is a reasonable minimum, with monthly reviews for complex payrolls or after an incident. Payroll

articles.summary: Employee Management Employee Benefits in Nigeria: A Complete Guide for Employers Nikhil Thakur September 7, 2026 Employee benefits in Nigeria have now become a deciding factor for employees to make decisions on staying on a job. Beyond salary, candidates now ask for Health plans, Pensions plans, and other benefits the business plans to offer to make them feel comfortable. This guide covers what the law actually requires, what employees genuinely care about, and how to manage all of it. What Employee Benefits Actually Are Employee benefits are everything your employee receives beyond their base salary. The pension deduction on their payslip. The HMO card in their wallet. The annual leave days they may or may not take. The salary advance they can access when things get tight. The December bonus they quietly factor into their household budget. Together, these form the total compensation package: what the job costs your business and what it is worth to your employee. Mandatory Employee Benefits in Nigeria Pension Contributions The employer contributes at least 10% of each employee’s monthly emoluments. The employee contributes 8%. That money goes into a Retirement Savings Account (RSA) with a Pension Fund Administrator (PFA) the employee selects. National Housing Fund (NHF) The NHF requires employees earning ₦3,000 or more annually to contribute 2.5% of their basic monthly salary into the fund. Annual Leave A minimum of six days of paid annual leave after 12 months of continuous service. Maternity Leave Female employees are entitled to a minimum of 12 weeks of paid maternity leave. Some are adding paternity leave provisions even without a legal requirement, because they understand what that signal means to the people on their team. NSITF and ITF The Nigeria Social Insurance Trust Fund (NSITF) and the Industrial Training Fund (ITF) both have contribution requirements depending on your business size. Non-Mandatory Benefits: Where You Actually Compete Health Insurance A functioning HMO is one of the most valued staff benefits in Nigeria and one of the most frequently broken ones. The plan sounds strong during onboarding. Then someone’s child is sick at midnight. They spend an hour trying to reach a helpline that does not answer, only to be told by a hospital that their cover has lapsed or is not recognised. Flexible Working In Lagos, a two-hour commute each way is normal. For someone moving between the Island and Ikorodu or from Mowe to the mainland, five days in the office means four hours lost daily. If possible, a flexible working plan is a great way to reduce employee stress and help them focus. Learning and Development Employees who see growth stay. Those who feel stuck start looking for whoever offers a course, a certification, or a path. You do not need a big L&D budget. A clear policy, a few sponsored certifications, and mentorship go far. Performance Bonuses Bonuses work best when they are clear. ‘You might get something if we have a good year’ is not a motivator; it is a vague hope employees learn not to plan around. Bonuses tied to defined outcomes, communicated clearly in advance, build both performance and trust. Employee Wellness Programmes Burnout costs you in sick days, low output, and good people who are present but not engaged. Employee wellness does not need to be complex. A mental health allowance, counsellor access, or flexible leave shows you see your people as people. Recognition The quietest driver of disengagement is invisibility. Employee rewards and recognition programmes do not require a large budget. They require consistency and intentionality. A structured employee rewards and recognition approach costs less than one resignation. The absence of recognition is not neutral. It costs you. Financial Wellbeing Financial stress is the loudest background noise in most Nigerian workplaces. Employers who offer real financial wellbeing support salary advances that process in days, access to short-term credit, and payslips that clearly explain every deduction build trust no bonus structure can create. How to Structure Market-Competitive Allowances This sets your pension baseline and keeps PAYE tax exposure low. Basic Salary: Typically comprises 40% to 60% of gross pay. Housing Allowance: Accounts for 15% to 30% of the gross package to handle high urban rental costs. Transport Subsidy: Typically ranges from 10% to 15% of gross pay to offset heavy commuting expenses. 13th-Month Pay: Not a legal requirement under the Labour Act, but heavily expected as an end-of-year bonus in December. Why Employee Benefits in Nigeria Are a Retention Strategy Most business owners never calculate this: what does it cost to replace one employee? Recruitment fees or management time spent sourcing if you go direct. Multiple interview rounds. Onboarding. Three to six months before the new person is productive. The institutional knowledge, client relationships, and context that left with the person who resigned. An all-in estimate for a mid-level hire runs between three and nine months of their salary. Compare that cost to your annual benefits budget. For most Nigerian businesses, a structured employee benefits package costs less than one urgent exit. An employee who is not worried about HMO, pension, or financial emergencies is focused at work. Focused employees make better decisions, move faster, and are less likely to be looking for a new job. And then there is the employer brand effect. Your candidates might talking to your current employees before they accept any offer. The way your team describes working at your company, in conversations you will never be in, is either your best recruitment tool or your biggest liability. Benefits are always part of that conversation. Where Nigerian Businesses Sometimes Get This Wrong These are the quiet patterns that erode trust over time: Offering Benefits Nobody Uses A gym partnership sounds like a solid perk until you realise 70% of your team don’t like going to the gym. Benefits disconnected from the actual lives of your employees are not effective. Ask your team what they want before you build the package. The Benefit Exists But Nobody Knows This is common. The HMO details is buried
articles.title: Employee Benefits in Nigeria: A Complete Guide for Employers
